FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state:

Japanese Encephalitis in Andhra Pradesh 
*304. PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether, according to a newspaper report published in the Indian Express dated 
3rd November, 2000, Japanese encephalitis is killing a number of children every year 
in Andhra Pradesh; if so, 
5 

RAJYA SABHA [16 March, 2001] 
whether Government have taken enough precautions to stop this 
disease from showing its ugly face this year; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is a fact that Government came across vaccine and medicine 
shortage in this regard last year; and 
(d) if so, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C.P. THAKUR): 
(a) to (d) As per reports re ceived from Andhra Pradesh Health Authorities, 343 cases 
of Japanese Encephalitis with 72 deaths were recorded in Andhra Pradesh during last 
year. No separate data on cases and deaths of children is available. The Directorate of 
National Anti-Malaria Programme has issued detailed guidelines suggesting various 
measures for strengthening the surveillance activities for controlling the Japanese 
Encephalitis. Preventive measur es undertaken for control of Japanese Encephalitis 
include:— 
—strengthening of surveillance activities; 
—identification of treatment centers in ende mic districts besides district hospitals; 
—vector control measures by undertaking residual insecticidal spray with appropriate 
insecticides in high risk areas; 
—fogging with Malathion for killing of Japanese Encephalitis mosquito vector 
during outbreaks for containment of morbidity and mortality rate; 
—anti-larval operations; 
—early diagnosis and proper management of patients; 
—health education to increase public awareness; 
—segregation of pigs from human population; 
—training to medical personnel and profes sionals associated with delivery of 
preventive and control activities in the field of Japanese Encephalitis; 
While no shortage of medicines was reported by the Government 
6 

[16 March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
of Andhra Pradesh, supply of JE vaccine was less with reference to the demand of the 
State Government. However, the Central Research Institute (CRI) Kasauli, which is 
the sole manufacturer of the JE vaccine in the country, could meet over 60% of the 
demand for this year. The Goverament of Andhra Pradesh has been asked to intimate 
firm annual demand of the vaccine in the ne xt 5 years so that Institute can gear itself 
for higher level of production of the vaccine. 
Further, due to sudden increase in the demand of the vaccine and limited 
production capacity of the CRI, Kasauli, the Government of Andhra Pradesh was 
advised to consider the possibility of import of JE vaccine by using the good offices 
of WHO. 
Hunting of Prohibited Animals 
† * 305. SHRIMATI SAROJ DUBEY: Wi ll the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that a la rge number of prohibited animals are 
hunted every year by the hunters; 
(b) if so, whether Goverament are going to take any steps to prevent such 
hunting; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. BAALU): 
(a) A number of poaching cases are detected 
by the State Governments and Regional Deputy Directors, Wildlife Preservation, 
Government of India every year. 
(b) and (c) The steps taken by the Government to prevent illegal hunting are: 
(1) Steps taken at the State level: 
(i) Legal protection has been provided to wild-animals against hunting and 
commercial exploitation under the provisions of 
the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. 
(ii) State level and District level coordination committees have  
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
7 

RAJYA SABHA [16 March, 2001] 
been set up in several States to prevent poaching and illegal trade in wildlife. 
(2) Steps taken at National level 
i.   Government of India has set up Regional and Sub-regional Offices for wildlife 
preservation in major export and trade centres of the country to prevent 
smuggling of wild-animals and their products. 
ii.    Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) has been empowered under the Wildlife 
(Protection) Act, 1972 to apprehend and prosecute wildlife offenders. Anti-
poaching efforts are being coordinated with INTERPOL. 
iii.  Financial and technical help is be ing extended to the States under various 
Centrally Sponsored Schemes, viz. Project Tiger, Project Elephant, 
Development of National Parks and Sanctuaries and Eco-development around 
Protected Areas for enhancing the capacity and infrastructure of the States for 
providing effective protection to wild-animals. Financial assistance is, in 
particular, being provided for raising 'Strike Forces' and providing arms to the 
protection staff for combating the organised poachers. Assistance is also 
provided for giving rewards to the in formers for elicitin g information about 
poachers and smugglers. 
iv.   A Special Coordination and Enforcement Committee has been set up under the 
Chairmanship of Secretary, Environment & Forests, Government of India, for 
control of poaching and illegal trade in wildlife. 
v.    Export of wild-animals and their derivatives is prohibited under EXIM policy. 
vi. A National Conference of Forests and Environment Ministers of State 
Government was held on 29th and 30th January, 2001. It was resolved to 
organise existing protection staff into viable formations for effective control of 
poaching and to create enforcement infrastructure both within and out side 
protected areas. 
8 

[16 March, 2001] RAJYA  SABHA 
vii. Ministry of Home Affairs has written to all- the State Governments to lend a 
helping hand to the field formations to curb poaching and illegal trade in 
wildlife. 
Steps taken at International level. 
i.  Government of India seeks International co-operation under the provisions of 
the Convention on International Trade in  Endangered Species of Wild Flora 
and Fauna (CITES) for control of illegal trade in wildlife items. 
ii.  A Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with Nepal has been signed by 
India to establish a joint Task Force to check the trafficking across the 
borders. 
iii.   Indo-Chinese Protocol in tiger  conservation Article of the protocol inter-alia 
stipulates joint measures to crackdown illegal activities of poaching of tigers, 
smuggling and selling the tiger bones and other parts of the tiger as well as 
its derivatives. 
iv.  A Global Tiger Forum of Tiger Range Countries has been created for 
addressing international issues related to Tiger Conservation. 
(d) Does not arise.

Deaths during Child Births 
*307. MISS FRIDA TOPNO: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether India tops the list of deaths during child births, as stated by Mr. Allan 
Cort, a UNICEF representative; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) what steps Government have taken/propose to take to prevent the same? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C.P. THAKUR): 
(a) Based on the data on Ma ternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) provided by the Sample 
Registration System—1998, of the Registrar general of India, it is estimated that about 
1.1 lakh women in India die every year due to causes related to pregnancy and child 
birth. According to the data published by UNICEF in its publication on 'The State of 
the World's Children 2001', 30 countries have maternal mortality ratio higher than 
that of India. In terms of the absolute numbers, however, India which is the second 
largest country in the world, reports highest number of maternal deaths. 
(b) The main causes of maternal deaths are: 
1. Direct Causes: haemorrhage, infections, Obstructed Labour, Unsafe Abortion, 
Toxemia of Pregnancy etc. 
2. Indirect Causes: Anemia, Viral Hepatitis, Tuberculosis and Malaria. 
3. Socio-economic causes: Early age of marriage, adolescent pregnancy, low 
status of women, low level of female education, lack of access to health 
services, gender bias and economic dependency. 
(c) Maternal health care is an integral part of the Family Welfare 
Programme. Certain vertical interventions like National Nutritional 
10 

[16 March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
Anemia Control Programme and Tetanus Immunisation Programme for pregnant 
mothers have been going on under the Family Welfare Programme since 1977-78. In 
1992, the nationwide Child Survival and Safe Motherhood (CSSM) (1992^97) was 
launched with World Bank support, for integrating various vertical interventions in the 
area of Maternal and Child Health. The Reproductive and Child Health (RCH) 
Programme, which was launched in 1997 for five years, continues the CSSM 
activities along with certa in new programmes. The major interventions of RCH 
programmes aimed at bringing down maternal, infant and child mortality are: 
1. Provision of Essential Obstetric Care 
2. Provision of Emergency Obstetric Care 
3. Provision of services in backward dist ricts by holding RCH Camps at Primary 
Health Centres. 
4. Contractual appointments of additional ANMs for backward districts. 
5. Provision   of   contractual   or   part   time   appointment   of 
Anaesthetists, Gynaecologists, Safe Motherhood Consultants and technical 
staff like Laboratory Technicians, Public health Nurses etc. 
6. Provision of drugs and equipment for Ma ternal Health at sub-centres, primary 
health centres, community health centres/first referral units—including Iron 
and Folic Acid tablets for maternal and childhood anemia. 
7. A scheme for 24 hour delivery services at selected primary health centres and 
community health centres. 
8. Referral transport for pregnant women for eight backward states. 
9. Facilities and training for medical termination of pregnancies for safe abortions. 
 
10. Prevention,  management and control of Reproductive Tract Infections (RTI), 
Sexually Transmitted Infections (STI). 
11. Intensification of Information, Education and Communication 
11 

RAJYA SABHA [16 March, 2001] 
Programmes for Maternal and Child Health through the mass media as also 
decentralised local specific activities at the grass root level. 
12.   Involvement of NGOs in awareness generation and service delivery where 
government services are not adequate. 
13. Training of medical/paramedical and other service 
providers. 
14. Training of Dais. 
The need for bringing down MMR considerably and improving maternal 
health in general, has been strongly stressed in the National Population 
Policy—2000, which has recently been approved by the Government. This 
policy recommends a holistic strategy fo r bringing about total inter-sectoral 
coordination at the grassroots level an d also for involving the NGOs, civil 
society, Panchayati Raj Institutions and women's groups in bringing down 
MMR and Infant Mortality Ratio.

*314. VEN'BLE DHAMMAVIRIYO: Will the Minister of MINES be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Supreme Court, in the case of R.K. 
Sabharwal Vs, State of Punjab, has held that Vacancy Based Roster can operate only 
till such time as the representation of persons belonging to reserved categories reaches 
the prescribed percentage of reservation; and 
(b) if so, the services in classes / grades under Ministry of Mines all 
the Public Sector Undertakings and subordinate offices under its 
control where representation of persons belonging to SC/ST 
categories has reached the prescribed percentage of reservation, 
leading to replacement of Vacancy Based Roster by Post Based 
Roster? 
THE MINISTER OF MINES (SHRI SUNDAR LAL PATWA): (a) Yes, Sir. As 
per the Supreme Court judgement (R.K. Sabharwal Vs. State of Punjab), reservation 
has to be with reference to posts and not vacancies. A post-based roster is a 
mechanism to ensure that the reserved categories get their due share of posts upto the 
prescribed percentages of reservation for the concerned categories in line with the 
principles enunciated in the aforesaid Supreme Court judgement. 
(b) In pursuance of the judgement of the Supreme Court (R.K. Sabharwal Vs. State 
of Punjab), Department of Personnel & Tr aining (DoP&T) have issued guidelines 
vide their O.M. No. 36012/2/96-

Decline In Elephant Population 
2251. SHRI CM. IBRAHIM: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news report which 
appeared in the Indian Express dated the 11th February, 2001 under the caption "They 
want poachers-get fifth dead elephant"; 
(b) if so, how the elephant population has declined during the last five years and 
this year, indicating elephants' population, births and deaths since 1996-97, onwards; 
and 
38 

[16 March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) what steps have been and are being taken to piotect and promote this 
endangered and majestic animal? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. BAALU): 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Overall population of elephants in the country, including deaths and births, has 
increased from 25,571 in 1993 to 28,665 in 2000. 
(c) Elephants have been included in the schedule-I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 
1972 which prohibits their hunting. The Act was further amended in 1986 and 1991 to 
prohibit trade in ivory. Export of ivory from the country is also banned. A centrally 
sponsored scheme "Project Elephant" was launched in Febraury, 1992 to provide 
financial and technical assistance to the el ephant-bearing States for conservation of 
elephants and their habitats. Government of India has so far provided State 
Governments about Rs. 44 Crores under this Project. Recently, the Central 
Government has also empowered the C.B.I, under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 
to apprehend and prosecute the wildlife offenders. A Special Co-ordiantion and 
Enforcement Committee has been set up under the chairmanship of Secretary, 
Environment & Forests, Government of India, for control of poaching and illegal 
trade in wildlife. The matter relating to protection of wild animals was also discussed 
in the conference of the State Forest Ministers in Coimbatore in January, 2001 and the 
following recommendations for improving the existing protection system were made: 
 
1. Lifting the ban on recruitment of forestry personnel and filling up the vacancies 
immediately. 
2. Evolving effective mechanism  for intelligence gathering and preventing 
wildlife crimes. 
3. Training for the forest staff for undertaking investigation. 
4. Designating special courts for trying wildlife offences. 
5. Creation of effective enforcement infrastructure both within and outside 
protected areas to prevent poaching.

(b) to (d) It has been informed that on 6.2.2001 one Sri Samuel, Plantation whatcher 
while perambulating Nagaluty Forests in Bairluty range of Atmakur division in 
Nagarjunsagar Srisailam Tiger Reserve had seen the carcass of a Tiger in Gosaikatta 
tank abetting the reserve forests. He alerted the Forest Range Officer, Nagaluty, who 
rushed to the spot after informing the Di visional Forest Officer, Atmakur, who was 
attending to sales in Velgode. The Divisional  Forest Officer rushed to the spot along 
with Field Director (Project Tiger) Srisaila m. The carcass was lying in pool of water 
on the dried banks of Gosaikatta tank with the skin intact and three (3) of the paws 
removed. There was a mark on the neck with deep would suggesting that the tigress 
has died due to noosing. After preliminar y investigation the ca rcass was shifted to 
Bairluty to conduct postmortem. Postmortem was conducted by Assistant Director-
Veterinary, Atmakur on 7-2-2001 confirming the preliminary report of death due to 
strangulation. A UDOR case was booked by Forest Range Officer, Nagaluty vide No. 
73/2000-01, Dt. 6-2-2001, and the Police has also been informed of the same. The 
Chief Wildlife Warden, A.P., rushed to the spot on 7-2-2001 to assist the 
investigation by the field officers. 
On 7-2-2001, five (5) teams of Forest & Police Officials have 
thoroughly inspected the scene of offence. Sniffer dog was also pressed into service 
for investigation, and the dog led the team to the house of one Sri Dammari Srivarma.

care of zoo animals to be adhered to.

be provided to them.

zoos was also agreed to. 
Killing of Elephants 
2265. SHRI CM. IBRAHIM: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the article captioned 
"Elephants are Dying" appearing in the Hindustan Times on 21st January, 2001; 
(b) if so, whether Government are aware of the new method adopted by elephants 
killers for the sake of tuskers and other precious parts of his body; and 
(c) the number of elephants who died or we re killed, reserve-wise, during the last 
three years and the steps taken to effectively prevent killing of elephants? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. BAALU): 
(a) and (b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) According to the information provided by the state Governments, 146 
elephants were killed during the last thr ee years. Reserve-wise information is not 
available. 
Elephants have been included in the Schedule-I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 
which prohibits their hunting. The act was further amended in 1986 and 1991 to 
prohibit trade in ivory. Export of ivory from the country is also banned. A centrally 
sponsored scheme "Project Elephant" was launched in February, 1992 to provide 
financial and technical assistance to the elephant bearing States for conservation of 
elephants and their habitats. Government 
57 

RAJYA SABHA [16 March, 2001] 
of India has so far provided State Governments about Rs. 44 Crore* under this 
Project. Recently, the Central Government has also empowered the C.B.I, under the 
Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 to appreh end and prosecute the wildlife offenders. A 
Special Coordination and Enforcement Committee has been set up under the 
chairmanship of Secretary, Environment & Forests, Government of India, for control 
of poaching and illegal trade in wildlife. The matter relating to protection of wild-
animals was also discussed in the conference of the State Forest Ministers in 
Coimbatore in January, 2001 and the following recommendations for improving the 
existing protection system were made: 
1. Lifting the ban on recruitment of forestry personnel and filling up the vacancies 
immediately. 
2. Evolving effective mechanism for intelligence gathering and preventing 
wildlife crimes. 
3. Training for the forest staff for undertaking investigation. 
4. Designation special courts for trying wildlife offences. 
5. Creation of effective enforcement infrastructure both within and outside 
protected areas to prevent poaching.

2296. SHRI KHAGEN DAS: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Tuberculosis has assumed epidemic form in some parts of the country; 
(b) whether there is any shortage of funds and drugs to tackle this problem; and 
(c) what steps have been taken to create fa cilities for effective treatment of T.B. 
patients and the results thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) No, Sir. The number of TB cases reported under 
National TB Control Programme (NTCP) have been more or less same during the last

(b) No, Sir. 
(c) Under National TB Control Programme (NTCP) drugs are provided to all the 
TB patients, free of cost, through the primary Health Care infrastructure. 
A Revised National TB Control Programme (RNTCP) has been in operation since 
March, 1997. Under this Programme, the Directly Observed Treatment—Short 
Course (DOTS) Therapy recommended by WHO has been adopted for more effective 
and complete treatment. In RNTCP districts, one Microscopy Centre has been set up

a cure rate of more than 80% in sputum smear positive cases.

Budgetary allocation for Primary Education 
2313. SHRI MOHD. AZAM KHAN: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether compulsory and free education for every child between six to fourteen 
years of age is a fundamental right but Government have not yet worked out the 
expenditure required for this; 
(b) whether some sources have put this at three per cent of Gross Domestic Product 
(GDP); 
(c) if so, whether this percentage is correct; 
(d) whether provision in Budget is only 3.2 per cent at present; if so, how 
Government plan to fulfil the goal and do it properly; and 
(e) what is Government's thinking about emphasis on value education and 
whether State-sponsored religious education is contrary to the spirit of our 
Constitution? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOU RCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. MURLI 
MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) The Hon'ble Supreme Court has declared education up to 
the age of 14 years to be a fundamental right. The recently approved programme of 
Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan allows States/Districts to plan for universal elementary 
education through a community owned process of preparation of Distt. Elementary 
Education Plan as per broad national norms. The actual requirement of resources will 
depend on the District Elementary Education Plans. All efforts to provide resources 
as per approved plans would be made. 
(b) and (c) The Saikia Committee (1997) estimated an additional requirement of 
Rs. 8000 crores per year. The Tapas Majumdar Committee (1999) assessed an average 
annual additional requirement of Rs. 13700 crores. This is within 3% GDP assuming a 
modest growth rate in the economy. These assessments are approximate and the actual 
requirement can only be worked out by a community 
119 

RAJYA SABHA [16 March, 2001] 
owned process of decentralised planning. Assessment have also to take note of the 
private unaided sector in elementary education. 
(d) The Public expenditure including expenditure by all Ministries during 1998-99 
is 3.75% of GDP. Over and above this, there are investments from the private unaided 
sector in Elementary Education. The Central Plan Outlay for Elementary Education in 
2001-2002 stands at Rs. 3800 crores. This is substantially higher than what the Central 
Govt, had been spending in previous years. 
(e) The National Curriculum Framework circulated by NCERT has emphasized the 
need for Value Education. This includes inculcation of the basic values and an 
awareness of all the major religions of the country as one of the central component.

centric study on prostitution in six metropolitan cities viz. Bangalore, Chennai, Delhi, 
Hyderabad, Kolkata and Mumbai. According to the study, in Kolkata and Delhi, the 
age at the time of entry into prostitution in these cities is as under. 
Below 15 years 14.9% 
16—18 years 24.5% 
(c) The Government has formulated a National Plan of Action to 
120

combat trafficking and commercial sexual exploitation of women and children through 
strategies that cover prevention, legislation and law enforcement, provision of basic 
services to the victims of prostitution, rescue and rehabilitation, awareness generation 
and social mobilization. The Central Mini stries and State Governments would plan 
the interventions required and operationalise them. 
Apart from ensuring stricter enforcement of the provisions of the Indian Penal 
Code, the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956, and the Government is attempting

Poor condition of Indian children 
2325. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the newsitem captioned,. 
"Report on children to make dismal reading", appearing in Hindustan Times dated 27th 
December, 2000; 
(b) whether 53 per cent of India's children are malnourished and the figure is 
almost twice than that of sub-Saharan African countries which was the poorest region 
in the world; 
(c) whether the infant mortality rate in rural India continues to higher than that in 
urban areas and the gap between the Government policies for children and their 
implementation has widened; and 
(d) if so, what specific measures are being taken by Government to improve the 
children's conditions? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI SUMITRA MAHAJAN): (a) Yes, Sir, The 
Department is aware of the newsitem capti oned "Report on children to make dismal 
reading" appearing in Hindustan Times dated 27th December, 2000. 
(b) 53 percent of India's children were malnourished during the year 1992-93. The 
National Family Health Survey 2 conducted during 1998-99 reveals that 47% of 
children under 3 years of age are underweight which is not twice than the prevalence rate 
of malnutrition (31%) in Sub-Saharan African countries. 
(c) The infant mortality rate in rural areas continues to be higher than urban areas 
as per National Family Health Survey 2 (1998-99) findings. The infant mortality rate 
has been declining both in rural and urban areas and hence it may not be correct to 
say that the gap between the Government policies for children and their 
implementation has widened. 
(d) The Government is seized of the problem and is implementing a   number   of   
interventions   through   its   different   sectors.   The

Mantri Gramodaya Yojana, Nutrition Educat ion and Extension, National Plan of

JAYSINGHRAO GAIKWAD PATIL): (a) Yes, Sir.

Optimisation Technology for Mineral Processing Plants" has been approved by the

Abandoning Townships after Mining 
2347. SHRI C. O. POULOSE: Will the Minister of MINES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that in normal circumstances a raining township is 
destined to die when a mining company depletes the mineral resources and leaves for a 
new location, resulting in social and economic disruption in old township; and 
(b) if so, what policy Government have contemplated for broad base activities and 
sources of employment in abandoned township? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF MINES (SHRI JAYSINGRAO 
GAIKWAD PATIL): (a) and (b) Under the National Mineral Policy, 1993, it has been 
provided that mineral deposits being exhaustible, once the process of economical extraction 
of a mine is complete, there is need for its closure. Whenever mine closure becomes 
necessary, it should be orderly and systematic and so planned as to help the workers and 
the dependent community rehabilitate themselves without undue hardship. 
It is known quite in advance before the actual closure of the mines that the mining 
activity in the area would cease. The mining lease holding companies facilitate smooth 
transition through a policy of offering voluntary retirement as well as absorbing the 
surplus personnel to the extent feasible in other units of the mining Company, and in 
some cases also undertake career counselling on alternative means of employment. The 
community facilities and services maintained by the mining company are also gradually 
handed over to other service providers, including the State Government concerned.

2367. SHRI PARMESHWAR KUMAR AGAR WALLA: Will the Minister of 
RAILWAYS be pleased to state what are the terms of agreement signed between India and 
Bangladesh in respect of rail link established between the two countries? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS (SHRI 
DIGVIJAY SINGH): There are following five operational Rail links between India and 
Bangladesh:— 
1. Gede (India)—Darsana (Bangladesh)—Broad Gauge. 
2. Singhabad (India)—Rohanpur (Bangladesh)—Broad Gauge. 
3. Radhikapur (India)—Birol(Bangladesh)—Meter Gauge. 
4. Mahisasan (India)—Shahbazpur(Bangladesh)—Meter Gauge. 
5. Petrapole (India)—Benapole(Bangladesh)—Broad-Gauge. 
Interchange of traffic between India and Bangladesh is governed by Rules of Interchange 
agreed to by Ministry of Railways. Government of India and Bangladesh Railways, 
Government of Bangladesh and Train Working Agreement executed by the two Railways for 
each rail link. 
The salient features of these Agreements are as under:— 
1. Only freight traffic is permitted to be interchanged between the two countries at 
present. 
2. Train Working is limited to only daylight hours, i.e. between sunrise and sunset. 
3. Wagons of either country will be allowed to be interchanged. Wagon hire charges 
will be payable based on the average net wagon balance. 
4. Both railways will recover freight char ges for the distance travelled in their 
respective countries by trains moving between India and Bangladesh following 
paid to pay system.

have been nominated for each rail link.
